traverse.c: TRAVERSE. There is also a Partition of art Escutcheon us ’ d in Heraldry of this Figure, which they call Parted per Pale Traverse. Argent and Gules,

TRAVERSE, is also a Word much used in Answers to Bills in Chancery or it is that which the Defendant pleadeth Or faith in Bar, to avoid the Plaintiff ’ s Bill, either by confessing or avoid - ing, or By denying and traversing the material parts thereof. '.. “ To traverse an Office, is nothing else but to prove, That ah Inquisition made of Lands Or Goods by the Escheator, is defective, and untruly made. And to traverse an Indictment, is to take Issue upon the chief Matter, and to contradict or deny feme Point of it.

TRAVERSE, in fortification, is a little Trench bordered with two Parapets, vi. One On the fight Side, and another on the left, which the Besiegers make quite thwart the Moat of the Place, to pass secure from Flanf - ihot, and to bring the Miners to the Baftiofis. This Traverse is usually covered op top with Hurdles or Bavins laden with Earth, for Security from the Fire - works, and differs from a Coffer only in this refpedl, That it is made by the Befie - gers, and the other by the Besieged. This Word is now Often us ’ d for any Retrench - ment or Line Fortify ’ d with Fascines, Gabions Barrels, Bags of Earth, &c.

TRAVERSE - Bo r, is a little round Board hanging up in the Steerage of at Ship, and bored full of Holes upon Lines Showing the Points of the Compass upon it, by moving of a little Peg from Hole to Hole, the Steers - man keeps an account how many GialTes ( that is, half Hours ) the Ship Steers upon any Point.

traumaticks.c: TRAUMATICKS, afe those things which be - ing taken in Decodlions and Potions, fetch the fe - rous and sharp Humours out of the Body, and so attenuate the Blood, that it may be conveniently driven to the wounded, broken, or bruised Parts. Blanchard.

treason.c: TREASON, is of two lorts, vi. High and Petty Treason. High Treason is defined to be an Offence committed against the Security of the King or Kingdom, whether it be by Imagination, Word or Deed as to compass or imagine the Death of the King, Queen, or Prince or to De - iiower the King ’ s Wife, or his eldest Qaughter tjn. married, or his eldest Son s Wife or levy Wat against the King in his Realm, adhere to his Ene - mies, counterfeit his Great Seal, Privy Seal, or Money: To Kill the King ’ s Chancellor, Treasurer, Justices of either Bench, Justices in Eyre, of Af - size, or of Oyer and Terminer, being in their Place, doing their Office diminiftiing or impair - ing current Money, arid many others, as may be seen in divers Statutes particularly express ’ d. In case of this Treason, a Man shall be Hang ’ d, Drawn Und Quartered, and forfeit his Lands and Goods to the King. It is sometime called Treason Para - mount, Petty Treason. See the Word it self in its proper place. There is also mention of Accumulative Treafonj and Conjlruftive Treason, in the Statute Car. cap.. And here Note, That in Majori proditicne bones sunt principales, there are no Acceflaries in Treason, all are Principals. And Voluntas non re - puiabitur pro faclonif in causa Proditionis, for Petty, ' ajon

treasure.c: TREASURE - TROVE, is when any Money, Gold, Silver, Plate, or Bullion is found in any, Place, and none knows to whom it belongs then the " Property thereof belongs to the King, but the Civil Law gives it to the Finder, according to the Law of Nature. The Punishment for concealing Treasure found, is Irnprifonment and Fine. But if any Mine or Metal be sound in any Ground, that always pertains to the Lord of the Soil, except it be a Mine of Gold or Silver, which used to be al - ways to the King, in wjiofe Ground soever it be. found: But by a late Ad of Parliament, the King; hath only the Preemption.

treble.c: TREBLE, is the last or Bigfieft of the four Parts in Mufcal Proportion.

treenels.c: TREENELS, in a, Ship, are long Pins or Nails of Wood, whence they are called Tree - tells, or Tree - nails, made out of the Heart of Oak, to fa - llen the Planks to the Timbers and these have always Oakam, driven into them to prevent any. Leak.

treesandshrubs.c: TREES and Shrubs, of our Native Growth in England, are thus diftinguiffied by our molt Judi - cious Botanist, Mr. John pay. I. Such as have their Flower disjoined and remote from the Emit and these are, . Nuciferous ones, or such as bear Nuts, as the Walnut Tree, the Hazel Nut - tree, the Beach, the Chefnut, and the common Oak. . Coniferous ones, or such as bear a Iquammofe or scaly Fruit, of a kind of Conical Figure, and of a woody or hard Substance, in which are many Seeds, which when they are Ripe, the Cone opens or gapes, in all its leVeral Cells, andPartitions, and so they drop out. Of this kind are the Scotch Firs, Male and Female the Pine, which in our Gardens is called the Scotch Firrj the common Alder Tree, and the Birch Tree. . Bacciferous ones, or such as bear Berries as Juniper, and the Yew Tree. . Lanigerous ones, or such as bear a woolly downy Substance j as the black, white, and trem - being Poplar, Willows, and Ofiers of all kinds. . Sucfe f R I T R E . Such as bear their Seeds ( ' having an immersed Flower ) in Leafy Membranes or Cales; as the Horn - beam or Hardbeam, called in some places the Hornbeecb. II. Such as have their Fruits and Flowers Conti - guous and these are either with the Flower placed on the Top of the Fruit, or else have it adhering to the Base or Bottom of the Fruit. . Trees and Shrubs with the Flower placed on the Top or Upper - part of the Fruit: Of these, some ate Pomiferous, as Apples and Pears; and some Bacciferous, as the Sorb or ServifeTree; the White or Haw Thorn, the wild Rose, Sweet - brier, Cur - rants, the great Bilberry Bush, Honey Suckle, Ivy, &c. . Trees whose Flower adheres to the Base or Bottom of the Fruit, are either such as have their Fruit moist and soft when Ripe, as . Pruniferous ones, whose Fruit is pretty large and soft, with a Stone in the middle; as the black Thorn or SIow - Tree, the black and white Bullace Tree, the common wild Cherry - Tree, the Black Cherry, &c. z. Bacciferous ones; ar the Strawberry Tree, in the Weft of Ireland, Miffeltoe, Water Elder, the Dwarf a large Lawrel, the Viburnum or way - faring Tree, the Dog - berry Tree, the Sea black Thorn, the Berry - bearing Alder, the Pri - vet Barberry, common Elder, the Holly, the Buck Thorn, the Berry - bearing Heath, the Bramble and the Spindle Tree, or Prick - wood. Such as have their Fruit dry when ’ tis Ripe; as, the Bladder Nut - Tree, the Box - Tree, the com - mon Elm and All, the Maple, the Gaule or Sweet - Willow, common Heath, Broom, Diers Weed, Furze or Gorse, the Lime - Tree, &c.

tremor.c: TREMOR, is a voluntary Motion depraved, by which the Member is sometimes raised up, and sometimes depressed through the mutual Contra - ction between the Faculty and the Part affected.

trenchesinfortification.c: TRENCHES, in Fortification, are certain Moats or Ditches, which the Besiegers cut to approach more securely to the Place Attack ’ d, and are of fe - veral forts, according to the different nature of the Soil ‘ for if the adjacent Territory be Rocky, the Trench is only an Elevation of Bavins, Gabions, Wool - packs, or Shouldrings of Earth cast up round about the Place: But where the Ground may be easily open ’ d, the Trench is dug therein, and bor - der ’ d with a Parapet on the Side of the Besieged. j The Breadth of it ought to be from to o Foot, and the Depth from to. These Trenches are to be carried on with wind - j ing Lines, in some manner parallel to the Works of the Fortress, so as not to be in view of the Ene - my, nor to expose its Length to their Shot, which they call Enfilading for then it will be in danger of being Enfiladed, or secured by the Enemies Cannon: And this carrying of the Trenches ob - liquefy, they call, carrying the Trenches by Coudees or Traverses. They call it Opening the Trenches, when the Be - sieges begin to Work upon the Line of Approaches and this is usually done in the Night, and some - times within Musket - shot, and sometimes within half or whole Cannon - shot of the Place, if there be no riling Ground about it, the Garrison Strong, and their Cannon well served. The Workmen that open the Trenches, are always Supported by Bodies of Men against the Sallys of the ‘ Besieged; and sometimes those Bodies lie between them and the Place, as also on their Right and Left. The Pioneers sometimes Work on their Knees, and the Men that are to support them, lie fiat on their Fa - ces, in order to avoid the Enemies Shot: And the Pioneers are also usually covered with Mantelets or Saucijfons. They also fay, Mount the Trenches j that is, go upon Duty in them: And to Relieve the Trenches, is to Relieve such as have been upon Duty there. To Carry on the Trenches, is to ad - vance them towards any Place.

trepanum.c: TREPANUM, the lame with Mediolus which fee.

trespass.c: TRESPASS, signifies any Transgression of the Law under Treason, Felony, or Mifprifion of either for a Lord of the Parliament to depart from thence without the King ’ s Licence, is neither Treason nor Felony, but Trespass. But this Word is most commonly tiled for that Wrong or Damage which is done either to the King in his Forest, or by one private Man to ano - ther; and according to this Signification, it is of two forts; Trespass General, otherwise called Tref - pass vi & armis; and Trespass Special, otherwise called Trespass upon the Case and this seemeth to be without Force, howbeit they are sometimes confounded. How to distinguish the Forms of these Writs or Addons, fee F. N. B. Sol.,. In an Adion of Trespass, the Plaintiff always Sues for Damages, or the Value of the Hurt done him by the Defendant. There is also Trespass local, and Trespass transitory. Trespass local, is that which is so annexed to the Place certain, that if the Defend - dant join issue upon a Place, and traverse the Place only by saying absque hoc, That he did the Trespass in the Place mentioned in the Declaration, and aver it, it is enough to defeat the Adion. Tref - pass Transitory, is that which cannot be defeated by the Defendant ’ s traverse of the Peace, because the Place is not material: But the Adion of Trespass puare clausum fregit, ought to be Local.

tressed.c: TRESSED - TREES, in a Ship, are those Tim - bers of the Cross Trees that stand along Ships, or Fore and Aft at the tops of the Masts. See Cross Trees,

tressure.c: TRESSURE, a term in Heraldry. for an Orle when it is flowered; and if there be two of them, it is called a double Tressure. See Orle.

trifrima.c: TRI Frima, are Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury, the Three Hypostatical Principles of the Chymifts, out of which they pre ( nd that all mix ’ d Bodies are compounded, and into which they are ulti - mately resolvable by Fire; but the latter is false, and the first impossible to be proved.

trialinlaw.c: TRIAL, in Law, is used for the Examination of ail Causes, Civil and Criminal, according to the Laws of the Realm, before a proper Judge: Of which there are divers kinds; as Matters of Sad ( hall be tried by the Jurors; Matters of Law, by the Justices; Matters of Record, by the Re - cord it self. A Lord pf Parliament, upon an In - didment of Treason or Felony, hall be Tried without any Oath by his Peers, upon their Ho - U hours T R I T R I hours and Allegiance; but in Appeal at the Suit of any Subject, they shall be Tried per bonos & legates homines. If ancient Demelne be pleaded of a Mannor, and denied, this shall be Tried by the Record of Doomsday. Bastardy, Excommenge - i ment, Lawfulness of Marriage, and other Eccle - fiaftical Matters, shall be Tried by the Bishop ’ s Certificate.

triangularcompasses.c: TRIANGULAR Compasses, are such as have three Legs or Feet to take off any Triangle at once; they are used in Maps, Globes, &c.

triangularquadrant.c: TRIANGULAR Quadrant, is a SeBor, with a loose piece to make it an Equilateral Triangle; the Calendar is graduated on it, with the Sun ’ s Place, Declination, and many other useful Lines, and by the help of a String and a Plummet, and the Di - vision graduated on the loose Piece, it may be made to serve fof a Quadrant.

triangulare.c: TRIANGULARE OJfculum, the Triangular little Bone, is that which is placed betwixt the Lambdoidal Suture of the Skull, and the Sagit tails. Blanchard.

triangularisamuscle.c: TRIANGULARIS, a Muscle of the Thorax, which with its Partner, lies on each side the Car - til ago Ensiformis, within the Cavity of the Tho rax, under the Sternum sometimes this appears to be three, at other times four distinct Muscles on each side. It arises from the Inferior part of the Os PeBoris, whence its upper part ascends, and lower defends to its Implantations at the Bony endings of the fourth, fifth, sixth, and some - times seventh and eighth Ribs, near their Con - junction with their Cartilages. Its reputed Ule by moll ( if not all ) Anatomists, is to contract the Bread.

triceps.c: TRICEPS, is a Muscle of the Thigh, so called from its three Heads or Beginnings, the fird and larged of which, ariseth broad and fleshy from the Inferior Edges, and External Parts of the Os Jfchi - um, and Pubis, where they are joined to each other lying between the Semi - tendinojfus, and Semi - mem. - branofus, and that of the Gracilis, and descending with an Oblique Order of fleshy Fibres, is insert - ed partly Tendinous and Fleshy, near an Hands length in breadth to the Linea Aspera, of the Thigh bone, that is immediately below the Inlemon of the Quadratus Femoris its Inferior part making a Arong round Tendon, inferred into the Superior part of the Internal and Lower Appendix of the Thigh - bone. The second Head, or beginning of this Muscle, ariseth Tendinous from the CL Pubis, but in its de scent soon becomes Fleshy, and joins with the for - ’ mer, near to its Insertion to the middle part of the Lined aspera of the Thigh - Bone. The third and lad beginning of this Muscle, springeth from the Inferior part of the Os Pubis, betweeri the Origination of its lad defcnbed Head, and that of the PeBineus; and descending Cbhque - ly, joins with the fird near its Insertion io the Li nea Aspera of the Thigh - bone, immediately above the Termination of the second Head cf this Muscle This moves the Thigh variously according to the diversity of its Beginnings j so the fir it described part pulls the Thigh - bone upwards, inwards, and - somewhat backwards: The second and third Be - ginnings of it, pull it more inwards, and turn it somewhat outwards, as when we put our Legs a - cross each other.

tricuspides.c: TRICUSPIDES are three Valves of a Trian - gular form, placed at the Mouth of the Right Ven - triple of the Heart; they are made of a thin Mem - brane, and their Bases are fixed to the Mouth of the said Ventricle, and their Points tied by small Fibres to the Fleshy Productions; so that when the Heart contra & s, its Point approaches its Basis, and the Fleshy Productions move upwards; therefore the Fibre's of these Valves are relaxed, and the Valves lifted up by the Blood which gets under - death them, because the Furrows and Fleshy Pro - ductions keeping the Valves at a little di - dance from the Sides of the Ventricle, give way to the Blood to pass under them, and so to thrud up the Valves, which shut so closely the entry into the Ventricle, that the Blood cannot return the way it came in, but when the Ventricle is dilated, the Fibres are pulled down, and the Passage made open for the Blood to enter.

trigonometry.c: TRIGONOMETRY is the Art of Measuring Triangles, or of Calculating the Sides of any Tri - angle fought; and this is either Plain or Spherical: Of which I shall speak distil & ly; beginning first with the Plain. The Art of Trigonometry doth much depend on the Knowledge of the following Lines in and a - bout a Circle. . The Difference of any Ark from a Quadrant be it more or le Is, is called its Complement. Thus O F is the Complement of the Ark O T, being what it wants of being a Quadrant; and O F is aho the Excels by which the Ark O D exceeds a Quadrant; the Line r is the Right Sine of the Complement, and therefore ’ tis called the Co - Sine r Sine - Complement of the Ark O T; as O R Is the Co - Sine of the Ark F O. v . A Line, asTS, touching the Circle in the point T, and Perpendicular to the Radius C T, is - called a Tangent: And if a Right Line be drawn through O from the Centre of the Circle C, meet - ing with the Tangent in S, that Line S C is called a Secant, and they both limit one another, so as to be the Tangent and Secant of the Ark O T: F N is the Co - Tangent, and C N the Co - Secant of the fame Ark - but they are the Tangent and Secant of the Complemental Ark O F. ’ a ' . K The Line R T intercepted between the Right Sine and the Tangent, is called the Versed Sine, and by some Sagitta. . Whatever Number of Degrees an Ark wants of a Semi - circle, is called its Supplement. . The Line C R, which is the part of the Radius C T lying between the Centre and the Right Sine, is always equal to, and may be taken for the Co - Sine r O and C r is equal to the Right Sine OR. . If any Ark bless than a Quadrant, as T O; the Difference between the Radius and the Co - Sine, is the Versed Sine R T but if it exceed a Qua - ck ant, as the Ark D F O doth then the Sum of the Radius and Co - Sine, is the Versed Sine: ThuS ' DC - f CR “ DR the Versed Sine of the Ark D F O. . The Radius with the Sine and Co - Sine of any Ark ( as T O ) do make a Right - angle Trian - gle, as O C R, which is similar to the Triangle C S T, made by the Radius, the Tangent, and the Secant. Also the Radius, the Co - Tangent, and the Co - Secant, make another Triangle similar to the two former. DEFINITIONS. I i. The Line D T in a Circle, is called the s Diameter, one half of which, C T, as also C O, and C F, is called the Radius; and by some the whole Sine, because all other Sines are taken out of it. . z. Any Right - line, as O A,, joining the two Ex - tremities of an Ark, is called the Chord, or Sub - Hence tense, either of the Ark OT, or of its Comple - ment to a whole Circle O D A. . The Line O R, which is Perpendicular to the Radius C T, or which is just half the Chord O A, is called the Right - fine, or most usually the Sine of the Ark O T, or of the Ark O D, so that a Right - fine is half the Chord of double the ArkJ T R I T R I As Radius is to the Sine:; fb is the Secant to the Tangent. Every Triangle has fix Parts, of which three are Sides, and three Angles j and of these if we have three given, we can find the reft, ( except in the Case where the three Angles only of a Plain Triangle are given. ) For from thence the Sides cannot be found, be - cause two Triangles may be Equiangular, and yet have the Sides by no means of the fame length. We can find the reft, I fay, if supposing the Radi - us divided into any Number of equal Parts, we can but discover how many of such parts any Sine, Tangent, or Secant of any Ark or Angle doth con - tain. Nov / this is ready done to our Hands, in the Table of Signs, Tangents, and Secants, which we have, with prodigious Industry, in Books rea - dy calculated for this purpose. a. When therefore any Triangle is given to be resolved, the first thing we have to do, is to cqnfi - der. Triangles proposed. . A Spherical Triangle is made by, or contained under the Arks of three great Circles of the Sphere. Definition l A Spherical Angle, is the mutual Inclination or Aperture of the Planes of two great Circles. Properties of Spherick. Triangles. f. When one Circumference of a Circle cuts, crosses, or falls on another, the Sum of the Angle made thereby is equal to two right ones. . When two Circumferences of Circles cross each other, the opposite or vertical Angles are al - ways equal. . In every Spherical Triangle, the greater An - gle is opposite to the greater Side. . An Isosceles Spherical Triangle, hath its An - gles at the Base equal to each other the Converse of which also is true, That if the Angles at the Bale are equal, the Triangle is an Isosceles. . If two Spherical Triangles are mutually Equi - lateral, they are also Equiangular and Similar one to another. . If two Spheric Triangles have in each one Angle and two Sides including it; or if they have one Side and two Angles adjacent respectively equal, the whole Triangles are equal. . Any two Sides of a Spherick Triangle, are lon - ger than the third because the Ark of a great Circle is the nearest Distance between any two Points on the Sphere. . All T R I T R f ; All great Circles must cut each other into two equal Parts because their common Inter - ietftion is a Diameter of the Sphere and conse - quently, the two Points of Interfe & ion are at the distance of a Semicircle from each other, COROLLARY, Hence ’ tis plain, That every Side of a Spheric Triangle must be less than a Semicircle. . The opposite Angles at the Intersection of two Circles are always equal, because the fame Planes constitute both Angles that is, the Angle a is equal to the Angle b, See Figure below, . In a Spherical ' Triangle, if the Sum of the Legs of any Angle be greater, equal, or less than a Semicircle the internal Angle at the Base is ac - cordingly greater, equal, or less than the outward and opposite one and consequently, the Sum of the two internal Angles at the Base is greater, e - qual or less than two Right Angles.

Nor is the Position of the Plane on which you take the Shade, or that of the Line thereon on which you measure the Recess of the Sun from the Tropick, very material; but in what way soever you dise ver it, the said Recess will be always in the fame Proportion, by reason of the smallness of the Angle, which is not Minutes in the first five Days: Nor need you enquire the Height or Distance qf your Building, provided it be very great, so as to make the Spaces you measure large and fair. But it is convenient, that the Plane on which you take the shade, be not far from perpendicular to the Sun, at least not very oblique; and that the Wall which calls the ftiade, be strait and Smooth at top, and its Direction nearly East and Weft. And it will be requisite to take the Extream greatest or least de - hiation of the shadow of the Wall, because the shade continues for a good time at a stand, without alteration which will give the Observer measure to be assured of what he does, and not be surprize by the quick transient Motion of the shade of a Angle Point at such a distance. The principal Obje & ion is, That the Penumbra or Partile ftiade of the Sun, is in its Extrearhs very difficult tO distinguish from the true ftiade, which will render this Observation hard to determine nicely. But if the Sun be transmitted through a Tele - scope, after the manner used to take his Species in a Solar Eclipse, and the upper half of the Object - glass be cut off by a Paper palled thereon, and the ead upper Limb of the Sun be seer just emerging oud of, or rather continuing the Species of the Wall, ( the Position of the Telescope being regulated by a fine Hair extended in the Focus of the Eye - glass ) then by this means the limit of the ftiade may be obtained to the uttiioft Exa & ness.

trover.c: TROVER, in LaW; is an Adrioh which a Man hath against one, that having found any of his Goods, refuses to deliver them upon demand. Of late, Adfions of Detinue are much turn ’ d into Addons upon the Case, Sur Trover & Convcrfion,

trough.c: TROUGH of the Sea, is the Hollow or Cavity made between any two Waves or Billows inarowl - ing Sea; and when a Ship lies down there, they fay, She lies in the Through of the Sea.

trucks.c: TRUCKS, belonging to the Carriage of a piece of Ordnance, are the Wheels which are on the Axle - tree to move the Piece.

trueplace.c: TRUE Place of a Planet or Star, is a Point of the Heavens fliewn by a right Line drawn from the Centre of the Eartji, through the Centre of the Planet or Star; whereat its apparent Place, is that which is found by a right Line drawn from the Observer s Eye through the Centre of the Planet or Star. And this Point in the Heavens is referred to the Ediptick or Zodiack, by the Planet or Star's Circle of Longitude,

truncated.c: TRUNCATED / r / zw / d or Cone, is one whole top is cut off by a Plane parallel to its Base; and therefore the Figure of the truncated top xnuft al - ways be similar to the Base. How to find its Solidity, see in the Word Fru jlrurti. A Truncated Cone, or the Frufirum of that Body is called fotnetimes a Curti - Cone.

trunkboots.c: TRUNK Boots of a Plant, are little Roots which break or grow out of the Trunks of Plants and are of two kinds. ! ft, Such as Vegetate by a direst Descent, the place of their Eruption being sometimes all along the Trunk, as in Mints, &c. and sometimes only in the utmost Point, as in Brambles; dly, Such as neither ascend nor descend, but ftioot forth at Right - angles with the Trunk; which therefore, tho ’ as to their Office they are true Roots, yet as to their Nature they are a Middle thing Between a Trank and a Root. Dr. Grew At, of Plants, p. s

trunnions.c: TRUNNIONS of a Piece of Ordnance, are those Nobs or Bunches of the Guns Metal which bear her up upon the Cheeks of the Carriages.

trusses.c: TRUSSES, are Ropes faftried to the Pari - els of a Yard in a Ship, lerving either to bind fast the Yards to the Mails, when the Ship rowls, lying either a Hull, ot at Anchor; or to Hale down the Yards in a Storm r Gust of Wind: They belong to the Main - yard, Fore - yard, and Missen, and are all brought to upon occasion.

try.c: TRY; a Ship is said to fry, when site hath no more fails abroad, but her Main - fail: When her Tacks are close aboard, the Bowlings fet up, and the Sheats haled dole aft; when also the Helm is tied dole down to the Board, and so Ihe is let lie in the Sea. And sometimes when it blows so hard, ? that they cannot maintain the Main - fail, as they fay; that is, cannot bear it out, they make h & lie a Try under a Miffenfail only, - a I Tube Fallopiana, are two slender Passages, proceeding from the Womb, which when they are a little removed from it, grow gradually wider: They have large Holes or Orifices, which almost lie shut, the extream Edges falling flat; yet if they be diligently opened and dilated, they represent the fextream Orifice of a Trumpet. Their Use is to receive the Eggs from the Testicles, and carry them into the Womb, according to the Excellent R. de Graefs the truth whereof is evident from the In - Ipeiftion of Rabbets differed.

tuber.c: TUBER, properly, is a subterraneous Must - foom, or a Truffle; but by Botanick Writers, is often used to signifie the round turgid Roots of some Plants: which therefore they call Tuberose Roots, or Kjiobby Ryots, as Mr. Ray Englifhes it.

tubuli.c: TUBULI LaUiferi, certain Lactiferous or Milk - carrying Pipes, which are as it were the Store - hole wherein the Milk is kept, and thro ’ which, as by Conduits, it flows to the Nipples of the Breasts of Females when they give Suck.

tubulivermiculares.c: TUBULI Vermiculares, are certain small wind - ing Cavities formed on the outside of the Shells of Marine Shell - Fishes, in which some small Worms inhabit and breed. These are very frequently found on such Foffll Shells as are dug up almost every where out of the Earth; and therefore help to demonstrate, that they are real Shells, and not formed Stones, as some will have it.

tuck.c: TUCK of a Ship, is the trussing or gathering up of her Quarter under Water; which if she lie deep, makes her have a Broad, or as they call it, a Fat Quarter, and hinders her fleering, by keeping the Water from passing Iwiftly to her Rudder; and if this Trussing lie too high above the Water, the will want bearing for her Works behind, unless her Quarter be very well laid out.

tumor.c: TUMOR; by this Word, which in general lig - nites any Swelling, the Chirurgeons understand a Disease or morbid Affecftion, incident molt usually to the Organical Parts of the Body, encreasing their Quantity preternaturally by Means of some fuperfiuous Humours coming thither from other parts.

tunicleinanatomy.c: TUNICLE, in Anatomy, signifies a Membra - nous Coat.

turbithmineral.c: TURBITH Mineral, or yellow Precipitate of Mercury, is thus made. Put any Quantity of good Quicksilver into a Glass Retort, and pour on it four times its weight of Oil of Vitriol. Set the Retort in Sand, and when the Mercury is dissolve ’ d, which ’ twill hardly be in ten Hours time, distil off the Humidity gently at first, but make a strong Fire at last, to drive out all the Spirits. When you break the Retort, you will find in it a white Mass, which pouder in a Glass Mortar, and then pour - ing warm Water upon it, it wall presently turn Tel - low; it must be walked several times, and dried in the shade, and then ’ twill Vomit and Purge strongly.

turiones.c: TURIONES; amongst Botanick Writers, are the first young tender Ihoots or tops which any Plants do annually put forth of the Ground.

turnaterm.c: TURN, a Term belonging to the Movement of a Watch, and signifies the entire revolution of any Wheel or Pinion. The number of Turns, which the Pinion hath in one turn of the Wheel, is commonly fet down as a Quotient in common Arithmetick, thus, ) ( where the Pinion playing in a Wheel of, mo - veth round times in one Turn of the Wheel. Now, by knowing the number of Turns, which any Pinion hath in one turn of the Wheel it work - eth in, you may also find how many turns a Wheel or Pinion hath, at a greater distance: as the Cert - rate - wheel. Crown - wheel, See. For, ’ tis but Multiplying together the Quotients and the Number produced, is the number of Turns, as in this Example. ( ) ( ) C The first of these three Numbers hath Turns ', the next, and the last. If you multiply by, it produceth; that is, in one Turn of the Wheel, there are Turns of the second Pinion, or the Wheel, which runs concentrical, or on the fame Arbor with the second Pinion. If you Multiply by the last Quotient, it produces, which is the number of Turns the third Pi - nion hath.

turn.c: TURN, is the Sheriff ’ s Court, kept twice eve - ry Year, vi. within a Month after Easier, and within a Month after Michaelmas. Magna Charta, cap.. From this Court are exempted only Arch - bishops, Bishops, Earls, Barons, all religious Men and Women, and all such as have Hundreds of their own to be kept. It is a Court of Record, in all things that pertain to it: It is also the King ’ s Leet through all the County, and the Sheriff is Judge; and this Court is incident to his Office.

TURN - P, in the Art of War, are Spars of Wood of or Foot long, and about Inches diameter in a hexangular Form: They are bored with holes, one right under another, about an Inch diameter; the Axis of each hole must be fix Inches one from another, but to go by turns from each side, the Pickets that are driven into the hole, are or Foot long, pointed with Iron, and with Wedges or Nails fatten'd hard into the holes. Two of these fatten ’ d together with an Iron Chain and Staple, some Inches long, will be of great use ro flop the Enemies in the Breaches, or elsewhere. But those that are intended to be thrown in Breaches, must be made of Oak, and need not be so big, or the Pickets so long.

turnoviceccmitiim.c: TURNO Viceccmitiim, is a Writ that lies for those that are called to the Sheriff's turn out of their own Hundred.

tuscanorderofarchitecture.c: TUSCAN Order of Architecture; so called, be - cause Invented in Tufcany, an eminent Part of Italy Tis the most plain of all the, and is seldom us ’ d but in some Country Building, where there is no need of any Order but one; or else in some very great Building, such as an Amphitheatre, or the like where all the Orders are design ’ d to be used. The Columns here, together with Base and Ca - vital, are to be Modules in Length, and to have their Thickness diminish ’ d by degrees to a quarter part. When these Columns stand alone, the ( paces between them or the Inter - columns ought to be very large. Their Pedefials ought to be one Module high; and the Base of the Column ought to be of the Height of half its Thickness; and that Height di - vided into two equal parts, ij kes the Orle or Plinth T Y M T Y R Plinth, which is made with a kind of Compass; the other is divided into parts, of which, one is for the Lift, the. other for the Tore, or thick round Circle of the Pillar. The Base hath a Sail / e or Bearing out, which is the th part of the diameter of the Column. The Capital is an. Height half the thickness of the Column at the Base; and is divided into three equal parts, ( according to O anam ) of which, one is for the Abacus, the other for the Oeuft, as they call it in French, i. e. the Ornament and the third part being divided into Divisions,, thefirft makes the Lift under the Ornament; and the other fix serve for the Gorgerin Collier, or Frife. The Aftra - gal is the height of the Lift below the Orna - ment.

tuscanwork.c: TUSCAN Work, in Architecture, is the most simple and rude of the Five ancient Orders of Pil - lars. See Column and Order.

twilight.c: TWILIGHT, is that dubious half Light which we perceive before the Sun - rising, and after Sun - setting. ’ Tis occasion ’ d by the Earth ’ s Atmosphere and the splendor of the / Ether which environs the Sun. The Ethereal accended Atmosphere of the Sun, not setting so soon as, and riling before the Sun; and the Sun ’ s Rays also illuminating the Earth ’ s Atmosphere, before the Body of the Sun it self can appear, occasions a Light always piece - ding at the rife, and subsequent to the setting of that Planet. Which, tho ’ because of many acc - dental Variations in both the Sun ’ s and Earth ’ s At - mosphere, it cannot be always of the fame degree of Duration or Brightness; yet it usually holds in the Evenings, till the Sun is about Degr. below the Horizon, and appears so long before his Rife in the Morning. And therefore will be least un - der the Equator, where the Sun rises and sets at Right - angles to the Horizon; and so Will encrease more and more, according as the Position of the Sphere grows more oblique: For, in our Latitude, for a good part of the Year, the Sun is never above Degrees below the Earth; and conse - quently, all that time we have no Night, but con - tinkal Twilight.

tympaninarchitecture.c: TYMPAN, in Architecture, is that part of the bottom of the Frontons, which is enclosed be - tween the Cornices, and answers the Naked of the Fri e.

tympan.c: TYMPAN of an Arch, is a Triangular Table placed in its Corners. The most simple of these T ympans, have only a Table hollow ’ d, sometimes with the Branches of Lawrel, Olive - tree, or Oak, or with Trophies, and are conformable to the Dor ick and Tonic k Or - ders. But the riches, are adorn ’ d with flying Fi - gures, as Fame, or fitting Figures, as those of the Cardinal Venues, and are proper for the Corinthian and Compofit Orders. Tympan, is also attributed to the Pannels of Doors in Joyners Work, and to the Dye or Square of Pedestals

tympanitestympanias.c: TYMPANITES, Tympanias; the Disease call ’ d a Tympany; is a fix ’ d, constant, equal, hard, re - filling Tumour of the Abdomen, which being beat or struck, yields a found. It proceeds from & stretching Inflation of the Parts, and of the Mem - branaceous Bowels, whose Fibres are too much Iwoln with Animal Spirits, and hindred from re - ceding by the Nervous Juice, which obftrudls the Passage; to which Difternper, there is consequent - ly added, as the Complement of all, an abundance of flatulent Matter in the places that are empty. Blanchard.

tympanum.c: TYMPANUM, br rather Tympani Membrana, the Drum, or the Skin of the Drum of the Ear, is a small, thin, orbicular, transparent, nervous and dry Membrane, of most exquisite Sense, stretched over the Cavity of the inner part of the Ear, and dividing ( between the inward and outward Ear. Some Will have it to spring from the Pericranium, o - thers from the Dura - mater, others from the Pia - mater, and others from the softer Process of the au - ditory Nerve, there expanded; and there are some Anatomists, which believe it hath a Substance pro - per to its self, made in the first Formation of the Parts, and springing from nothing else. It is very dry, that it may give the better found; and ft ring, to bear external Injuries the better. It is enchased in a Channel made in the circumference of the outer end of the Bone that joins to the Cartilage which forms the largest part of the Meatus Auditorius; and it hath a Cord Which runs ac'rofs it behind, which some take for a Ligament to strengthen it; but Vejney faith, ’ tis a Branch of the th pair of Nerves which supplies Twigs to the Muscles that move the Tympanum, which are two in Number, When this Membrana Tympani is taken away, there appears a Cavity on the inside of it, which is properly the Tympanum, but Verney will call it the Barrel. It ’ s about a quarter of an Inch long, and half an Inch wide; ’ tis compassed, found with Bone, and clad within with a Membrane, which is interwoven with a great number of Vessels. How Sounds are diftinguifli ’ d by means of this Membrana Tympani, and the four Bones Malleolus, Incus, Stapes, and the Os Orbiculare, you will find at large under the Word Ear.

tympanuminmechanicks.c: TYMPANUM, in Mechanicks, is a Cylinder, ' but larger and ftiorter than the common Axis or Cylinder, which is the Axis in Pgritrochio, and ’ tis usually placed upon that Axis, and is much the fame with the Peritrochium, which is a kind of Wheel placed on the Axis, in whose Circumference are Staves or Levers to turn the Axis easily about, in order to raise the Weight required. ; TYPHODES, is a Symptomatica !, continued burning Fever; as it were, from the Inflammation of the Bowels. Blanchard.

typhomania.c: TYPHOMANIA, is a Delirium with a Phrensy and a Lethargy. Blanchard.

typusorperiodusandcircuitus.c: TYPUS, or Periodus and Circuitus, is the order that intermitting Fevers observe, confiding of In - tension and Remission, ofEncreafing and Decrea - sing, according to some kind of Regularity; and accordingly denominating the kind of the Fever, by its Type. Blanchard. TYROSlS, is when Milk which is eaten. Cur - dles in the Stomach into a Substance like Cheese; Blanchard, A V A - C VAC ? V A L A CATION, by the Lawyers, is all the respective time betwixt the end of one Term, and the beginning of another. It signifies also the time from the Death of a Bi - fhopj or other Spiritual Person, till the Bifhoprick, or other Dignity, be supplied with another.

tallage.c: TALLAGE, is a Feedue for Cloths brought for sale to Blackwell - HaB in London - and also the Toll that is due to the Lord of a Fair or Market, for such Goods as are vended in the Common Hall of the Place.

TALLAGE, was formerly a certain Rate or Proportion, according to which Barons and Knights were Tax ’ d by the King, and inferior Tenants by their Lords. And this latter Tallage of the Customary Tenants was sometimes fix ’ d and certain, and sometimes at the Arbitrary Plea - sure of the Lord; and it was also sometimes Com - pounded for.

taberdersortabiters.c: TABERDERS, or Tabiters, for so by Cor - ruption ’ tis now pronounced, are the Batche - lor Scholars of the Foundation of Queen ’ s in Oxon: They were so called from a ihort Gown, called Taberd, or Tabert in those days, reaching no lower than their Middle - leg; which these Batchelor Scholars were then obliged to; wear.

tactics.c: TACTICS, is the Art of Disposing any Number of Men into a proper form of Bat - tle: The Greeks were very skilful in this part of the Art Military; having Publick Profeffors of it, who were called Taetici, who were to teach and inftrud their Youth in this Matter. JEllan hath a particular Book on this Subject, and there is a great deal of it in Arrian, in his History of Alex. M. and in Mauritius and Leo Imperator.

talussuperior.c: TALUS Superior, in Fortification, is the Slope on the top of the Parapet; for the Top of the Parapet is made Hoping, that the Solid - ers may defend the Covert - way with small Shot, which they could not do if it were le - vel.

tangentaplain.c: TANGENT, a Plain is said to be a Tan - gent to a Cone, when ’ tis Coincident with two Lines, one of which is drawn on the Sur - face of the Cone, and thro ’ its Vertex, and the other a Tangent to the Circle of the Base, meeting the former Line in the Point of Con - tact.

tangentline.c: TANGENT Line, how the Line of Tangents and half Tangents are made, you ’ ll find under Scales j and their Uses in Projecting and Mea faring the Parts of Eight Circles in Spherical Projection, you have under Spherick Projection. And the Use of the Line of Artificial Tangents, inConfort with the Line of Sines and Numbers you have in Plain Trigonometry, &c. But there are some ci - ther Uses of the Lines of Tangents and half Tan - gents in Dialling, cc. Sometimes on the edge of Gunter's SeCtor, you have a Tangent Line, in whose end a Pin or Gnomon, equal to Radius is Nor - mally placed; and by that means the Sun ’ s Altitude may be had, by holding the Sedov Ered, and the Pin Parallel to the Horizon; for then the Shadow of the Gnomon, when turned to the Sun will in the Divisions of the the Tangent ( hew the Degree of the Sun ’ s height.,, This Tangent - line is ufecl also to draw the Hour - lines on the Planes of Dials, and is com - monly known and shewn in almost all Books of Dialling. On the Cross - staff there are also Lines of Tan - gents drawn, one uftially of gm, and another of m which because their middle Points are at and, are by Mr. Gun ter called the Tangents of and. These Tangents are fifed in taking of Angles, the Altitude of the Sun or Scars, c. as you will find under Cross - jj: i - Dr. Wallis gives an Abftradf of his two Methods of Drawing Tangents to Curves, in Philosophical Tranfatlions, N.. which are ta - ken from his ConiclySeCtions, and other parts of his Mathematical Works. And Dr. Barrow, in his Fourth Geometrical Ledfion, y.. gives a gent - ral Method of Determining the Tangents to all Cycloid t, and all other Curves described, or gent - rated after the manner of a Cycloid. In Led:.,,. he shews how to determine Tangents to all ' manner of Spiral Curves, and to many Curves of Other kinds. In Philosophical Transactions, N.. you have a Method of Tangents, by Mr. H. Ditton, taken from the Theory of Maxi - ma and Minima, which is very Simple and Uni - versal.

tartan.c: TARTAN, is a fmallVeffel, much used in the Mediterranean, with but one Mali, and the three cornered Sail, like a Galley; they Fish with ihtm on the Coafts of S pain.

tassels.c: TASSELS, in a Building, are those pieces of Boards that lie under the Ends of the Mantle - trees.

taxers.c: TAXERS, are two Officers chosen in Cam - bridge, to look after the true Gage of ail Weights and Measures.

telescopes.c: TELESCOPES,; ( i. ) Sir If - Newton in his admiral - ble Treatise of Opticks, p.. demonllrates, that the Perfection of Hclsf copes is impeded by the different Refrangibility, of the pays of Light; and not as hath been vulgarly supposed, to the Spherical Figures of Glasses; and consequently, they will not be per - seated by Glasses of the Figures of the ConickSecli - ons, i. e. by Parabolick,, Hyperbolicly Glasses, c. For having shewed the Ratio between the less and greater Refractions of the different Rays to be ve - ry nearly, as to. He faith, those that are skilled in Opticks will easily understand, that the least Circular Space, into which the Object Glass - fes of Telefcopescan Collect all forts of Parallel Rays, is about the - part of half the Aperture of the Glass; or the th part of the whole A - aperture, and that the Focus of the most Refrangi - ble Rays, is nearer to the Object Glass than the Focus of the less Refrangible ones, by about ! part of the Distance between the ObjeCt Glass and the Focus of the mean Refrangible ones. And if Rays of all forts, flowing from any ono lucid Point in the Axis of any Convex Lens, be made by the Refraction of the Lens to converge to Points not too remote from theXewr, the Focus of the most infrangible Rays ( hall be nearer to the Lens than the Focus of the least refrangible Rays, by a Distance which is to the ‘ part of the DO fiance of the Focus of the mean Refrangible Rays from the Lens, as the Distance between that Focus and the Lucid Point from whence the Rays flow, is to the distance between Lucid Point and the Lens very nearly. After this, he shews by Experiments, made, with very great Accuracy, that the Rays of Light,: which differ in Refrangibility, do not all converge to the fame Focus y but if they flow from a Lucid Point as far from the Lens on the one side, as their Foci are on the other, the Focus of the most Re - frangible Rays ( hall be nearer to the Lens, than ? that of the least Refrangible, ’ by above the th part of the vvhole Distance: And if they flow from a Lucid Point so very remote from, the Glass, that - before their Incidence they may. be accounted Pa -, parallel, the Focus of. the most Refrangible Rays, shall be nearer to the. Lens, than the Focus of rule least Refrangible, by a th, or th, part of their whole distance from it. And the Diameter of the Circle in the middle Space between these two Fccit which they illuminate when they fall there on any Plane, Perpendicular to ' the Axis ( which Circle is the least into which they can all be gathered ) is a - boutthe th part of the Diameter of the Aperture of the Glass. So that ’ tis a wonder that Telescopes do represent ObjeCts so diftintely. - But were all the Rays of Light equally Refrangible,, the Error arising only from, the Sphericity of the Figures of Glasses, would be many hundred times - less. And expressly by Calculation, p.. he proves, that the Error arising from the Spherical Figure of Glasses, to that arising from the different Re - frangibility of the Rays, is as to, and consequently is so little, as defer ves not to bacon - fidered. There is another Argument ( faith our Excellent, ) Author, p.. ) which proves, that the different Refrangibility of the Rays, is the true cause of the Imperfection of Telescopes. For the Errors of the Rays arising from the Spherical Figures of the ObjeCt - Glasses, are as the Cubes of the Apertures of such ObjeCt - glasses: And thence to make Te - lefcopes of various Lengths Magnifie with equal Distinctness the Apertures of the ObjeCt - glasses, and the Charges or Magnifying Powers, ought tb be as the Cubes of the Square Roots of their Lengths; which doth not anfvver to Experience, But the Errors of the Rays arising from the dise - rent Refrangibility, are as the Apertures. of the Object - glasses: And thence to make Telescopes of various Lengths Magnifie - with equal Distinct - ness, their Apertures and Charges ought to be as the Square Boots of their Lengths And this an Evers to Experience, as is well known. For Instance, a Telefcopeof Feet in length, with an Aperture of Inches, Magnifies about times with as - much Distinctness, as one of a Foot in length, with ! of an Inch Aperture, Magnifies times. E By v / J -.... /, ., ) ' s Byreafon of this different Refrangibility, he concludes, that there can scarce be any other means ofimproving Telefcopesby Refractions alone, be - sides that of encreasing their Lengths j for which end the late Contrivance of Hugenius seems well accommodated ( fee Philosophical Tranfatiions N.. ) For in his Aerial Telescope the Glasses are readily manageable, and the Object - glass being upon a strong upright Pole, becomes more sea - dY Sir If. Newton, in his Opticas, p.. acquaints us how he Polished his Reflecting Metal, which he used in. his Reflecting Telescope; and vhich, because it appears to be a much better way than in any common use here give the Rea - der. I had two round Copper - plates, each of: fix Inches in Diameter, the one Convex, and the o - ther Concave, and ground very true one to ano - ther; on the Convex I ground the ObjeCt Metal or Concave which was to be Polished, till it had taken the Figure off the Convex, and was ready for a Polish, Then I Pitch it over thinly, by dropping melted Pitch upon it, and warming it to keep the Pitch soft, whilst I ground it with the Concave Copper, witted to make it spread evenly all over the Convex. Thus by working it well I made it as thin as a Groat, and after the Convex was cold, I ground it again to give it as true a Fi - gure as could. Then I took Putty, which I had made very fine, by washing it from all its gross Particles, and laying a little of this on the Pitch, with the Concave Copper, I ground it upon the Pitch till it had done making a noise, and then on the Pitch I ground the Object Metal with a brisk Motion, for about two or three Minutes, leaning hard upon it. Then I put fresh Putty upon the Pitch, and ground it again till it had done making a noise, and afterward ground the Objedb - metal upon it, as before; and this Work I repeated till the Metal was Polished, grinding the last time with all my Strength for a good while together, and frequently breathing upon the Pitch to keep it moist, without laying on any more fresh Put - ry. But because Metal is more difficult to Polish thanGlafs, and is afterwards very apt to be spoiled by Tarnilhing, and besides reflects not so much - light as Glass Quicksilver ’ d overdoes: I pro - pound, instead of Metal, to use a Glass ground Concave on the fore - side, and as much Convex on the back - side, and on the back - side well Quicksilver ’ d over; the Glass also must be exaCtly all over of the fame thickness, other - wife the ObjeCt will look Colour ’ d and Indi - ffinCt. Withfuch a Glass I tried about five or fix Years ago to make a Reflecting Telescope of four Feet in length, to Magnifie about times: And I fa - tissued my self, that there wants nothing but a good Artist to bring the Design to Perfection. For the Glass being only after the common manner of grinding Glasses for Telescopes, tho ’ it seem ’ d as g od as ObjeCt - glasses use to be, yet when it was Quicksilver ’ d, the Reflexion discovered innumera - ble Inequalities all over - the Glass: And by rea - fon of these Inequalities, ObjeCts appear ’ d Indi - stint in this Instrument. For the Errors of Refle - cted Rays, caused by any Inequality of the Glass, are about fix times greater than the Errors of Re - fracted Rays, caused by the like Inequalities. But I however found by this Trial, that the Reflexion on the Concave side of the Glass, which I feared would disturb the Vision, did really no sensible Prejudice to it; and confequendy, that nothing is wanting to persist these Telescopes but good Workmen, who can Grind and Polish Glasses tru - ly Spherical. I once mended a common fourteen Foot ObjeCt - glass considerably, by grinding it with Pitch or Putty, and leaning very easily on it in the Grinding, left the Putty Ihould scratch it; besides, leaning too hard on the Glass in Grinding it, is apt to bend it, and then the Figure cannot be truly Spherical. Sir Isaac Newton ’ s Method of short ’ ning Te - lefcopes. vid. his Opticks, p,. Let ade represent a Glass Spherically Concave on the Fore - side a h, and as much Convex on the Back - side c d, so that it be every where of an e - qual thickness for it must not be thicker on one side than the other, left it make Obje & s appear Coloured and Indiftindt; it must also be very well Wrought and Quicksilver ’ d over on the back - side. Place this Glass in the Tube v x y which must be made very black within. Let efg rere - sent a Prism of Glass or Chrystal, placed near the other end of the Tube, in the middle of it, by - means of an handle of Brass or Iron f g /, to whose end made flat it is Cemented. Let this Prism be Right - angled at e, and the other two An - gles exadlly equal, and confequentlyeach De - grees. Let the Sides e f and ge be exactly plane and Squares, and by consequence the third Side F G, a Re & angled Parallelogram, whose Length is to its Breadth in a Subduplicate Proportion of z to. And let the Side ef be turned to - wards the Speculum, and the Distance of this Prism from the Speculum, be such, that the Rays of the Light p q, r s, cc. which are Incident up - on the Speculum in Lines Parallel to the Axis thereof, may enter the Prism at the Side e /, and be reflected by the side fg, and thence go out of it thro ’ the Side to the Point t, which mull be the common Focus of the Speculum nb d cy and of a Plane Convex Eye - glass h, thro which those Rays must pass to the Eye. And let the Rays at their coming out of the Glass pass thro ’ a small round Hole, or Aperture made in a little Plate, Lead, Brass, or Silver, wherewith the Glass is robe co - vered; which Hole must be no bigger than is ne - celfary for Light enough to pass thro ’. For so it will render the Objedl diftindl, the Plate in which it is made, intercepting all the Erroneous Part of the Light which comes from the Verges of the Spe - culum ab Such an Inllrument well made, if it be Foot long ( reckoning the Length from the Speculum to the Prism, and thence to the Focus ?, ) will bear an Aperture of Inches at the Speculum, and Mag - nisi between i and times. But the Hole h, here limits the Aperture, with more advantage, than if the Aperture were placed at the Specu - lum. If this Inllrument be made longer or Shorter, the Aperture must be in proportion, as the Cute of the Square Root of the length, and the Magni - lying as the Aperture. But it ’ s convenient that the Speculum be at least an Inch or two broader than the Aperture; and that the Glass of the Spe - culum be thick, that it bend not in the Working. The Prism efg, must be no bigger than is neceffa - ry, arid its back - side / g must not be Quicksilver d over; for without Quicksilver it will reflect all the Light incident on it from the Speculum. In this Instrument the Object will be Inverted, ' but may be ere & ed by making the Sides e fr and eg of the Prism efg, not Plane but Spherically Convex, that the Rays may cross as well before they come at it, as afterwards between it and the Eye - glass. If it be desired, that the Instrument bear a lar - ger Aperture, that may be also done, by Come - lying the Speculum of two Glasses with Water be - tween them. The Reason why four Glasses in a Te - lefcope represent the Objedi ere eft, Mr. Mo - lyneux shews plainly in Philosophical Tranfatlionsl N.. Mr. Augout faith, in Philosophical TranfaclionSy N.. That the Apertures of Telescopes ought to be in a Subduplicate Ratio of their Lengths; but this must be taken, so as to allow for the Quantity of Light which comes into the Tube; for the more Light comes in the greater the A - aperture must be, faith Dr. Hoof. Ibid. And Dr - Hoof also doth there shew a way to make a Plano - Convex - glass of a small Sphere, colledl the Rays at a great distance j but I don ’ t find that he e ver made any considerable use of it after - ' wards. thunderandlightning.c: THUNDER and Lightning. The Phenomena of this very common, but oftentimes dreadful Meteor, are thus accounted for, and Solved by Dr. Hook. Opera Post. p., The'Atmofphere about the Earth abounds with Nitrous Particles of a Spirituous Nature, which are every where carried along with it; besides which fort of Particles, there are also others raised up into the Air, which may be somewhat of the Na - - ture of Sulphureous, Unduous, or other Combutti - ble Bodies; as we fee Spirit of Wine, Spirit of Turpentine, Camphire, and almost all other Com - buftible Bodies, will by Heat beRarinedinto the Form of Air or Smoak, and be raised up into the Air. All which, if they have a sufficient Degree of Heat, will catch Fire, or be turned into Flame by the Nitrous Parts of the Air, as thousands of Experiments might be brought, to prove. There are also other forts of these Sulphureous Steams, which arise from Subterraneous and Mineral Bo - dies, which only by their coming to mix with the Nitre of the Air, tho ’ they have no sensible Heat in them, will so ferment and ad one upon another, as to produce an dual Flame which is a thing that hath been often found in Mines, and more especially if any part of them be kindled, then the whole Train which is mingled with the Contiguous Air, will immediately take Fire, like & Train of Gun - powder, and run from one end of those Vapors to the other, be they never so long. As I could prove by a multitude of Relations from Coal - mines, and several other Mines. The Ac - cension of which Vapors is so sudden, and with such Violence and Swiftness, runs from one end to the other, as often to kill the Miners, blowup their Props, Turns, Stays, Houles, Pc, and produceth as prodigious Effeds, as if a vast quantity of Gun - powder had been fired in the Mine. Now Lightning in the Air seems to be much of the fame. Nature; for the Air is continual - ly fumifhed with Spirituous Nitrous Parts, and the Summer Heat, whenever extraordinary, raifis up out of the Earth ( and to this the Subterraneal Heat also is continually concurring ) a great quanti - ty of Sulphureous Vapours, which are of such a Na - ture, as that meeting with the Nitre of the Air, they work upon each other, and thereby begins a further Degree of Eleat, which gradually encrea - fes, till at last it arrive at a certain pitch; and then they fall upon and work on one another, pro - during an dual Fire and Flame, which with won - dernful Swiftness Fires the whole Train, and so pro - duces the Flafhand Noise. Dr. Wallis in Philcf. Trans. NQ. r. p., faith, That Thunder and Lightning are so very like the Effeds of fired Gun - powder, that we may reasonably judge they proceed from thelike Causes. Now the Principal Ingredients in Gun - powder, are Nitre and Sulphur ( the Admiftion of Charcoalbeing chiefly to keep the Parts separate, for the better kindling of it. ) So that if we sup - pose in the Air a convenient Mixture of Nitrous and Sulphurous V vapors, and those by Accident to take Fire, such Explofron may well follow with such Noise and Light, as in the firing of Gun - powder and being once kindled, it will run from place to place, as the Vapour leads it, like as in a Train of Gun - powder, with the like Effeds. This Explcfion, if high in the Air, and far frory us will do no mifehief, or not considerable, like a Parcel of Gun - powder fired in the open Air, where nothing is near enough to be hurt by it. But if the Explosion be near to us, oramongftus, it may T [ N T I D may kill Men or Cattle, tear Trees, fire Gun - pow - der, break Houses, or the, like; as Gun - powder would do in all like Circumstances. This Near - ness, or Farmfs, may be estimated by the Distance of Time between seeing theFlalh of Lightning, and hearing the Clap of the Thunder; for tho in their Generation they be Simultaneous, yet Light moving faster than Sound, they come to us successively. I haveobferved, that commonly the Noise is about seven or eight Seconds after the Flafli; but sometimes ’ tis much sooner, in a Se - cond, or two, or lefsthan that, just after the Slash, and then the Explosion mull needs be, very near us, and even amongst: us. And in such Cafes, I have more than once presaged the Expecta - tion of Mischief, and it hath proved according - ly. Now that there is in Lightning a Sulphureous Vapour, is manifest from the Sulphureous Smellthat attends it, and the sultry Heat in the Air, which is commonly a. forerunner of Lightnmgfoon after. And that there is a Nitrous Vapour in it, we may reasonably judge, because we do not know of any Body so liable to a sudden and violent Exploti - on. As to the kindling of these Materials, in order to such an Explosion, I am told, that a Mixture of Sulphur, and Filings of Steel, with the Admifti - on of a little W ater, will nor, only produce a great Effervefcen'e, but will of it self break forth into an actual Fire. I fay a little Plater, because too much will hinder the Operation, or quench the Fire: And this I take to be the Cause of the Bath Waters, and other hot Springs, where Steel and Sulphur cause a great Effervelcence, but no Flame. So that there wants only some Chalybeate or Vitriol - lic Vapour for somewhat equivalent ) to produce the whole Effect ( there being no want of Aqueous Matter in the Clouds. ) And there is no doubt, But that amongst the various Effluvia from the Earth, there may be copious Supplies of Matter for such Mixtions. The fame Account may also be given of JEtna, and ether burning Mountains, where the Mixture of Iron and Sulphur may give a Flame;. which is often attended with prodigious Explofions and Earthquakes from great Quantities of Nitre, as in Springing a Mine.
